summary.text: For Goldbach, write an even integer as twice its midpoint; after checking the cases with midpoint below 7 explicitly, positivity at the midpoint supplies two primes symmetric about it, whose sum is the original integer. For Lemoine, handle 7 as \(3+2\cdot2\), and for larger odd \(m\) apply positivity to the even number \(m-1\): a witness prime \(q\) makes \((m-1)-(2q-1)=m-2q\) prime, yielding \(m=(m-2q)+2q\).

full_proof.text:
Let us first state precisely what is assumed.

For a natural number \(n\), define
\[
 n^* = \begin{cases}
 1,&n\equiv 1\pmod 2,\\
 2,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The number \(A261627(n)\) counts the primes \(s<n+1\) for which, on writing
\[
 d=s n^*-1,
\]
one has
\[
 d<n,
 \qquad n-d\text{ prime},
 \qquad n+d\text{ prime}.
\]
(The inequality \(d<n\) ensures that \(n-d\) is ordinary, nontruncated subtraction.) Assume the A261627 positivity conjecture:
\[
 A261627(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>6. \tag{H}
\]
We prove both the strong Goldbach conjecture and Lemoine's conjecture.

## 1. Goldbach's conjecture

Let \(m\ge 4\) be even. Because \(m\) is even, write
\[
 m=2k
\]
for a natural number \(k\). The lower bound \(m\ge4\) gives \(k\ge2\).

We first dispose of the possibilities \(k<7\). They are exactly \(k=2,3,4,5,6\), and the corresponding even numbers have the following prime decompositions:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
k&m=2k&\text{decomposition into two primes}\\ \hline
2&4&4=2+2,\\
3&6&6=3+3,\\
4&8&8=3+5,\\
5&10&10=3+7,\\
6&12&12=5+7.
\end{array}
\]
All displayed summands are prime.

It remains to consider \(k\ge7\). Then \(k>6\), so hypothesis (H), applied to \(n=k=m/2\), says that \(A261627(k)>0\). A finite set has positive cardinality only if it contains an element. Consequently, there is a prime \(s<k+1\) counted by \(A261627(k)\). Set
\[
 e=\begin{cases}
 1,&k\equiv1\pmod2,\\
 2,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}
 \qquad d=se-1.
\]
By the defining conditions for an element counted by \(A261627(k)\),
\[
 d<k,
 \qquad k-d\text{ is prime},
 \qquad k+d\text{ is prime}. \tag{1}
\]
Take
\[
 p=k-d,
 \qquad q=k+d.
\]
These are prime by (1). Moreover, because \(d<k\), the subtraction in \(k-d\) is not truncated, and hence
\[
 p+q=(k-d)+(k+d)=2k=m.
\]
Thus every even \(m\ge4\) is the sum of two primes. Notice that the argument works regardless of whether \(k\) is odd or even: the definition may choose either \(e=1\) or \(e=2\), but in both cases it supplies two primes symmetrically placed around \(k\), and their sum is \(2k\). This proves the strong Goldbach conjecture.

## 2. Lemoine's conjecture

Let \(m\ge7\) be odd. We must show that
\[
 m=p+2q
\]
for some primes \(p,q\).

If \(m=7\), there is the explicit representation
\[
 7=3+2\cdot2,
\]
and both \(3\) and \(2\) are prime.

Now suppose \(m>7\). Put
\[
 n=m-1.
\]
Then \(n>6\). Moreover, since \(m\) is odd, \(n=m-1\) is even. In particular,
\[
 n\not\equiv1\pmod2,
\]
so the coefficient \(n^*\) used in the definition of \(A261627(n)\) is \(2\).

Apply (H) to this \(n\). Since \(A261627(n)>0\), there is an element \(q\) of the finite set counted by \(A261627(n)\). Thus \(q<n+1\) and \(q\) is prime, and, on setting
\[
 d=2q-1,
\]
we have
\[
 d<n,
 
 n-d\text{ is prime},
 \qquad n+d\text{ is prime}. \tag{2}
\]
Only the first of the two primes in (2) is needed for Lemoine's representation. Define
\[
 p=n-d=(m-1)-(2q-1).
\]
Then \(p\) is prime by (2), while \(q\) is prime because it was chosen from the primes counted by \(A261627(n)\).

It remains to check the desired identity without overlooking natural-number subtraction. The defining inequality \(d<n\) says
\[
 2q-1<m-1.
\]
Thus the quantities being subtracted are within range; equivalently, the subtraction in the definition of \(p\) is not truncated. Ordinary integer arithmetic therefore applies, giving
\[
 p=(m-1)-(2q-1)=m-2q.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 p+2q=m.
\]
Hence every odd \(m\ge7\) is a prime plus twice a prime, which is Lemoine's conjecture.

We have shown that assumption (H)—the assertion that \(A261627(n)>0\) for every \(n>6\)—implies both the strong Goldbach conjecture and Lemoine's conjecture.
